column2: A British proclamation has arrived at Pretoria. Sir Theophilus Shepstone claims that the republic's debts, frontier insecurity and military difficulties justify placing Transvaal under the Crown. Behind these arguments stands the confederation policy: London seeks to unite the southern African colonies and republics under imperial direction. On 12 April 1877, the historical republic lost its independence without a general battle. Our circumstances determine whether that proclamation can be enforced. A republic with a secured Mozambique corridor, recognised claims and a functioning coastal outlet can organise resistance on very different terms.
Receive the proclamation and convene the raad.

The proclamation is enforced, and the Union Jack rises over Pretoria. The Volksraad's sovereign authority gives way to a Crown administration, whose officials undertake to collect revenue and manage the republic's troubled finances. Farms, district offices and military units remain within British Transvaal, but the government no longer speaks as an independent republic. Acceptance today does not settle the question of consent. Petitions, deputations and meetings will carry the burghers' objections beyond the council chamber, while families weigh the cost of renewed resistance against the loss of self-rule. The occupied administration adopts its new public title and parties. It must now govern communities whose cooperation cannot be commanded by a proclamation alone, and whose memory of republican independence will shape every attempt at a lasting settlement.
Preserve the community beneath British administration.
A Republic with a Road to the Sea

Shepstone's claim meets an organised refusal. Our republic holds Ahoutburg, Andriesburg and the inland approaches as recognised territory, customs revenue and a coastal route have weakened the case that Transvaal cannot survive unaided. The commandos gather while the raad declares that no foreign commissioner may extinguish the independence recognised at Sand River. Britain now seeks by force the submission its proclamation could not obtain.

Petitions have failed to restore the republic. At Paardekraal, burghers renew their covenant to recover the independence taken in 1877. The triumvirate of Paul Kruger, Piet Joubert and Marthinus Pretorius gives political direction to the movement while district commandos prepare for the struggle. The declaration of 16 December 1880 opens the First War of Independence. Men who have kept their rifles and horses at home answer the summons, local knowledge and mounted mobility must offset Britain's greater resources. British suzerainty ends before war begins, allowing the conflict to reach a real military conclusion.
Restore the republic and fight for our freedom.
The Republic Vindicated: A Peace for the Burghers

The envoys return with the terms of peace, and the commandos gather beneath the republican colours. The long rides, guarded passes and anxious weeks on the farms have secured recognition of the burghers' right to govern their own country. Bells and thanksgiving services mark the news, but the raad must turn battlefield resolve into a lasting administration. Officials will restore the public accounts, receive the districts ceded under the treaty and arrange the withdrawal of the armies. The extraordinary mobilisation can now end, allowing families to return to their farms and workshops. Relations with Britain will require patience, for signatures cannot erase the memory of occupation and war. Let the country honour those who answered its summons, and let the peace they secured become the foundation of a durable republic.
Ratify the peace. Our republic shall govern itself!

Dispatches from the campaign have forced the imperial authorities to consider a negotiated settlement. Our commandos hold Pretoria and the key approaches through Natal, or Britain's exhausted expedition has failed to impose its will upon the republic's own districts. Continuing the fighting promises further losses and expense for both sides. The envoys offer restoration of republican self-government on the inland path, for the coastal republic, their terms also include the agreed frontier districts and the dependent Mabhudu administration. Britain would retain its remaining Cape possessions, and this limited agreement would end the campaign without the wider consequences of a complete Cape capitulation. The raad must decide whether these terms justify sending the burghers home, or whether to continue until a stronger settlement can be secured through the peace negotiations.
Accept the settlement and restore peace.
Continue until Britain accepts our terms through diplomacy.
The Republic Submits to Crown Authority

The peace negotiations have ended in Britain's favour. Our commandos have not secured the republic's independence, and the accepted terms place Transvaal under Crown authority. British officials return to Pretoria while Boer delegates seek guarantees for the districts, farms and institutions that survived the campaign. The extraordinary mobilisation ends, and the administration resumes its work under the title of British Transvaal, with the Union Jack and the parties of the occupied government. This is the immediate consequence of military defeat, not the final territorial settlement. Britain's conference must still choose between retaining a separate dependency, detaching its eastern acquisitions, or establishing direct colonial rule. For now, our communities remain under one administration as their representatives await the imperial decision. The memory of the republic will survive whichever arrangement is imposed.
Accept the terms and safeguard our people.

The Pretoria settlement restored Transvaal self-government under a qualified British relationship. In 1884, new negotiations at London revise that settlement. The republic secures firmer recognition of its independent administration while its external relations remain shaped by the conventions and the balance of power in southern Africa. The achievement belongs to diplomacy as well as to the commandos: a sovereignty defended in war must be maintained through treaties.
Record the convention in the republic's registers.

Cetshwayo's capture has ended the unified kingdom's resistance to Britain's invasion. On 2 September 1879, Wolseley's settlement partitions Zululand into thirteen chiefdoms under appointed authorities rather than annexing the whole country at once. The arrangement promises imperial oversight without the expense of a single administration, but it divides loyalties and leaves rivals competing for land, tribute and armed followers. At this game's scale the chiefdoms remain one Zulu tag under British suzerainty, their fragmentation is represented through administrative weakness and growing unrest.
Cetshwayo Returns to a Divided Kingdom

The partition has failed to bring peace. Britain permits Cetshwayo to return in January 1883, but not to the undivided kingdom he once ruled. His authority is confined by rival chiefdoms and imperial conditions, restoration under these terms cannot erase the struggles that the 1879 settlement created. The crown returns to a diminished monarchy beneath British oversight, as factions prepare to contest the next succession. Cetshwayo's return is a stage in Zululand's crisis, not a restoration of full independence.
Restore the king beneath the imperial settlement.

Years of partition, contested restoration and civil conflict have persuaded Britain to replace indirect supervision with direct rule. In May 1887, Zululand becomes Crown territory. The remaining Zulu administration is dissolved, while the lands of the recognised New Republic are treated separately. Direct annexation does not erase local society or the claims of the displaced kingdom, those communities now confront magistrates, taxation and colonial land policy. Administration through Natal will follow in 1897.

Boer volunteers have supported Dinuzulu in the struggle for the Zulu succession. Their victory at Tshaneni is followed by a grant of land, and on 16 August 1884 a new frontier republic is proclaimed with Vryheid as its political centre. Lucas Meyer and the settlers must turn promises into surveyed farms, public institutions and a defensible boundary. Recognition is narrow, and Britain will contest the republic's approach to the coast. This republic is distinct from Utrecht and Lydenburg: their earlier incorporation into Transvaal is not undone by the new settlement.
Recognise the frontier republic at Vryheid.

The small republic at Vryheid has found its ambitions constrained by disputed boundaries, scarce revenue and Britain's advance in Zululand. Its government now requests incorporation into the South African Republic. On 20 July 1888 the historical New Republic joined Transvaal, retaining a measure of district autonomy. The merger brings its administration and surviving territory under the republic's institutions, it does not revive the old Utrecht-Lydenburg union or surrender any coastal provinces held elsewhere.
The Tembe Frontier During the Zulu War

The Anglo-Zulu War has unsettled the frontier south of our Mozambique possessions. Tembe lies close to the coastal route through Ahoutburg, and the raad can seek a negotiated transfer to secure that approach. Acceptance will place the district under republican administration and recognise the republic's territorial claim. If the demand is refused, the raad must decide whether to pursue that claim through war.
Demand Tembe for the coastal frontier.

Transvaal's raad has proposed transferring Tembe into the republic's coastal administration. Republican envoys describe the district as a vulnerable approach to Ahoutburg, our council must weigh the pressure of the ongoing war against the cost of losing jurisdiction over its communities. A negotiated cession avoids another conflict. Refusal keeps the land but leaves the Boers a limited claim that they may choose to press.

The authorities holding Tembe have rejected the transfer. We may press a limited claim for the district, or accept the refusal and preserve peace. This is a claim to one province only: it must not become a war to annex an entire kingdom. War can be declared directly if the respondent is independent, if it is under British suzerainty, the claim must be pressed against Britain as the overlord.

The district register records the language of the administration holding the Tembe frontier. Republican administration uses the Dutch rendering Thembeland, a later change of authority restores the local designation.
Recognise republican self-government under the negotiated settlement.

Enforce the conference peace. Complete occupation of the British-held Cape must be recorded before peace to obtain the full Cape settlement. Otherwise only the limited frontier settlement is ratified.
Acquire Tembe only. No other provinces are annexed.

The war with Britain has ended without the special territorial settlement. The republic remains independent, but its commandos return to their districts and the extraordinary mobilisation arrangements are withdrawn. Peace alone cannot be treated as a military victory or used to claim land from neighbouring administrations.
Return to the work of the republic.
Imperial Protection Against the Coastal Republic

The coastal republic's refusal of Shepstone's proclamation has changed the diplomatic balance. British representatives offer the Zulu kingdom protection while they fight Transvaal, presenting imperial oversight as a defence against Boer frontier claims. Accepting joins Zululand to Britain's sphere of authority and exposes its districts to the result of the Anglo-Boer settlement. The king may instead reject the proposal and preserve his independence.
Accept British protection against the coastal republic.

A decade after direct Crown annexation, the administration of Zululand is incorporated into Natal. The change replaces a separate colonial arrangement with the institutions of the neighbouring colony. Communities confront Natal's magistrates, taxation and land policy, while the claims and consequences of the kingdom's destruction remain. At the game's national scale the land remains under the same British sovereignty, this event records the administrative change rather than another conquest.
